Houseplant ER

October 29, 2026October 29, 2026
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 8:57
Instaread

It doesn’t take a plant pathologist to know when a houseplant is in peril. Yellowing leaves, drooping stems, dropped flowers— these are all telltale signs your favorite piece of greenery is far from thriving. However, just because your plant is under the weather doesn’t mean it’s time to throw it on the compost pile: Most houseplants readily bounce back from the brink, if given the proper care and treatment. Here are common signs your plant needs some TLC, their causes, and how to treat them.

1). Yellow leaves – Over (or under) watering

This is one of the most common issues you’ll encounter as a plant parent, especially early on in your plant caretaking journey. Yellowed leaves are often a symptom of improper watering. Although this can happen when your plants don’t get enough water, it’s most often caused by overwatering.

Just as important as your watering regimen itself is the kind of container your plant resides in. If your planter has no drainage holes or is made of a non-porous material (such as plastic), water will accumulate at the bottom of your pot and cause all kinds of issues for your plant, some of which we will discuss later in this guide.

To treat yellowed leaves, pinch off the affected leaves at the base or stem of the plant, depending on the type of plant you’re working on. Stick a finger 1 to 2 inches into the soil to gauge the moisture. If the soil feels dry, water thoroughly until water leaks out the bottom (if you have drainage holes). If the soil is moist, lay off the watering for now, but continue checking the moisture level regularly. Once a day should be good to start off. When the soil feels dry over an inch below the surface, your plant is ready for a watering!

2.) Crispy, brown leaf edges – fertilizer burn

Have you ever lovingly fertilized a favorite houseplant, just to find the plant looking worse, not better, the following week? You’re far from alone: If your indoor plant develops brown, crispy edges, it’s most likely a sign of fertilizer burn.

As the name suggests, fertilizer burn occurs when too much fertilizer is added to a container. When your plant absorbs nutrients in the fertilizer, salts in the fertilizer pull moisture from the plant, resulting in the edges of the plant becoming dry, brown, and “burnt” in appearance.

Fortunately, fertilizer burn is generally a cosmetic ailment rather than a deadly one. If the burn is restricted to the edges of affected leaves, the rest of the leaf can still photosynthesize and help the plant grow. You can remove affected leaves from your plant through pinching or pruning. To prevent further fertilizer burn, avoid applying more fertilizer for at least a month. Going forward, try using half as much as you would apply regularly and observe how your plant reacts during the following week.

Other Causes for Browned Edges

If you have browned, crispy edges and don’t use fertilizer, you are likely dealing with one of two causes: too much sunlight or hard water. Check your plant’s lighting requirements online, and make sure you’re following recommended care instructions. Even inside, plants can experience sunscald and leaf scorch under certain circumstances.

Additionally, some plants (especially Calathea) are extra sensitive to minerals found in tap water. These divas get crispy edges easily if you don’t water them exclusively with distilled water, a fact vexingly left off most plant tags for the genus. Every so often, I pick up a gallon of distilled water at the supermarket just for my calathea.

3.) Dropping leaves – Light, Climate, and Location Changes

Speaking of houseplant divas, some plants (like Ficus) are known for readily dropping leaves as a response to changes in their environment. If you’ve recently moved your houseplant to a different part of your home (or, if your plant is located somewhere with fluctuating climate, such as near a drafty window), it isn’t uncommon for this to occur.

Another cause for leaf dropping is low light levels. For example, in my home I have a giant, oblong Schefferla (umbrella plant) sharing a window with a cat tree. Occasionally, the side of the plant that extends away from the window will drop a leaf or two, especially when I have the shade partially closed to keep it cool in the house. Ideally, this sun-loving plant should have a full window to itself, but my cat also longs to look out the window so I compromise.

Oftentimes, the best way to get your plant to stop dropping leaves is simply to wait out the issue. This is especially the case if you’ve recently moved your plant: once it acclimates to its knew location, it should put out some new leaves to make up for the dropped ones. If your plant is dropping leaves due to light, try rotating your planter so the affected side gets proper light, or move your plant to brighter location altogether.

4.) Stippling, dust, or specks on the plant – pests

No one likes finding bugs in their houseplants. Be it fungal gnats, thrips, spider mites, whatever: pests are always a pain to deal with, and are tempting to ignore altogether. Unfortunately, unless you’re content to let the colonies grow and fester, you ought to treat the issue before they become unmanageable and overwhelm both you and your plant collection.

Some pests are easy to spot, like fungal gnats. If you notice small, fruit fly-like insects flitting about your plants or on the planter, soil, or leaves, congrats: you have these stinkers! Fungal gnats are attracted to moist soil and decaying plant material, and feed off fungal mycelium growing in those environments. They are especially common in cases of overwatering and poor container drainage. These factors allow environments that allow fungal gnats to thrive.

To get rid of fungal gnats, you need a different approach when tackling the adults vs. the larva and eggs. Adult fungal gnats can be caught in sticky traps on your pots, or in light up traps plugged into a nearby outlet. As for the youth, kill them by prepping a mosquito dunk, then pouring the solution into infested pots with a watering can. I like to use mosquito bits for this part of the process.

Other pests are harder to see with the naked eye. Thrips and spider mites are both incredibly small but can be quite destructive nonetheless. These bugs both cause tiny specks on your plants, called stippling. This leads to an overall discoloration or “bronzing” of the leaf (see above image). Spider mites can also leave fine webbing on the underside of leaves if the infestation is severe. When left untreated, these infestations will spread quickly from plant to plant and eventually decimate your collection!

Never fear: pests can be easily managed with a combination of organic insecticides and integrated pest management (IPM) practices.

When I encounter pests on my plants, I spray the leaves with a diluted neem oil solution to take care of the issue. If however you have a large infestation across many plants, consider using biological control methods to remove the pests quickly and effortlessly. Releasing lacewing larvae into your plants is a surefire way to clear up most infestations naturally— ask your favorite local garden store if they have them in stock.

5.) Overlapping Symptoms on one plant – Root Rot

If your houseplant doesn’t respond to other treatment or is experiencing more than one sign of distress at once, it could be caused by a serious issue under the soil: Root rot. This ailment presents with similar symptoms to other common plant issues. Yellowed leaves, dropping leaves, brown edges, and even pests like fungal gnats are all associated with the condition. Furthermore, root rot causes stunted growth and an overall decline in plant health that can be lethal if untreated.

The cause of root rot is twofold: overwatering and poor drainage. When water pools in bottom of your plant’s container, the roots become waterlogged and susceptible to fungal infection. These mushy roots attract mold and fungi, which decay the roots and slowly kill the plant. Most plant parents only identify the condition when repotting an infected plant. Fortunately, this is also the perfect time to treat the issue!

When encountering root rot, it’s important to remove all affected roots before moving your plant to a new container. Use scissors or a small pruner to cut away any brown, mushy, or dead roots from your plant. Before replanting, ensure your plant’s new container has proper drainage holes, and fill your container with an appropriate soil for your plant type. For example, cacti readily develop root rot in standard potting soil; use a cacti soil mix for their containers instead. Going forward, water your plant on a schedule according to its specific needs.
